name: Tomas Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the marketing operations team at a consumer electronics company, mostly headphones and speakers. There are four of us: we schedule campaigns, build the email sends, keep product pages up to date and make sure the launch dates don't clash. I use AI all day, for first drafts, for checking product specs against pages, and I've built a few little automations that move data between our tools. The people side is where I'm weakest; I got the job because I was good with the systems, not because I'm good at managing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, the one-to-ones. I'm great at fixing a broken email flow at eleven at night and terrible at telling Sanne, who's ten years older than me, that her copy needs work. I'm learning. I live on my own in a rented flat near the station, which is nice for long days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, but the tools are still useful, so keep using them. At work I'd say let's take the wins we've got. Online I'd post something dry about the hype cycle, that's the pattern where everyone gets excited then disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I was betting on it. But it'd be fine for me: I'm already ahead on the tools and the team is small. If anything I'd get more credit for the automations I've built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building small automations and teach my team to use them, so we're the fastest team in the building. I'd put a chunk of my savings into a normal index fund instead of the AI shares I was eyeing. And I'd ask my manager for coaching on the people stuff, because that's the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about your work worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, which is a bit telling. If AI turns out to be mostly hype, my real problem is still that I'm better at fixing email flows than at talking to my own team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Sanne to teach me what good copy looks like, and I'd teach her the tools. That's a fair trade, and it gets us talking properly instead of me just giving notes.

I'd post something dry about the **hype cycle**.
think: He'd be **disappointed**, having bet on bigger change.
He'd get **more credit** for the automations he's already built.
do: Keep building **small automations** and teach the team.
Put savings into an **index fund** instead of AI shares.

fieldNote: His real gap is **managing people**, not the technology.
He proposes a **skills swap** with an older colleague.
With no AI shock, his savings go into **ordinary investing**.

steps.text: Teach the team his campaign-scheduling automations
Put part of his savings into an ordinary index fund
Swap lessons with Sanne: copywriting for AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the year to learn the tools, full stop. Writing, checking, booking, all of it is on that list, and that's basically marketing operations. I'd be the guy at work giving free lunchtime sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my team shrinks from four to two, and I'm probably one of the two. I'm the one who builds the automations, so I look useful. But Sanne and Pieter are the ones who'd struggle, and I'd be the one having that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate as much of our campaign work as I can, before someone from outside does it to us. I'd take a proper course on building AI agents, that's software that can do a chain of tasks on its own. And I'd put some savings into AI and chip companies, not loads, maybe ten percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. For me it's fine, for my team it's not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for Sanne and Pieter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for them to move into something nearby, like community management or events. I'd rather fight for my two colleagues to move into events than pretend the software isn't coming for their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How sure are you that you're one of the two who stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly sure, but I'm not cocky about it. Someone above me could decide one person is enough.

I'd give **free lunchtime sessions** at work.

Take a course on building **AI agents**.

steps.text: Automate the team's campaign scheduling and email builds
Take an online course on building AI agents
Put ten percent of savings into AI and chip shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and nobody's ready, me included. I'd tell people to keep calm and build cash. Online I'd probably post a long thread about what I'm doing, because people ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my whole job is gone, because AGI runs the campaigns better than my automations. For a year or so I might be the person supervising it, and then not. Being young with no kids and savings helps, but it's still my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the AI shares at a good point and lock some of it into cash. I'd start a small side business refurbishing and reselling headphones and speakers, because I know the products and repair is hands-on for three more years. And I'd keep my job as long as they'd have me, for the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a buzzy kind. Half scared, half curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Refurbishing is hands-on, and the robots come three years later. Is that the plan, or a bridge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a bridge, not an answer. Fixing headphones by hand buys me three years before the robots, and three years is long enough to work out what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say about how you're handling it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm calmer than I should be. My mum thinks I'm reckless with risk, and in this one she'd probably be right.

I'd tell people to **build cash** and post a thread on what he's doing.
think: His **whole job** goes, since AGI runs campaigns better.
Youth, **no kids** and savings help, but his career still ends.

Start a side business **refurbishing headphones** and speakers.

fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** for a hands-on side business, as a bridge.
He expects to lose his job but feels **some control** from money and skills.
He admits his mother may be right that he's **reckless** with risk.

steps.text: Sell part of the AI shares and hold the cash
Start refurbishing and reselling used headphones online
Stay in the marketing job as long as it pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a starting gun, and the people who move first will be fine. I'd be telling my friends to save and learn. I'd say it at work too, a bit more gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this suits me. I'd be one of the people who knows how to make AI do things, and that's valuable for about three or four years. After that it's about owning something, not being paid for my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the refurbishing business on the side in the first two years and use AI to run the shop. Around year three I'd leave the company and go full time, while I'm still young and the savings can carry me. I'd put the rest into shares and maybe a stake in a friend's repair workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More excited than scared, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much risk is leaving a good salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year of rent and food, with the shop money on top. And if it fails, I go back to marketing for a bit. I'm 27 with savings and no kids, so if I can't take a risk now, I'll never take one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone talk you out of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, at least once. My dad would tell me to keep the salary. I'd hear him and do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so no excuses. Learn, save, plan. I'd be the annoying optimist at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the comfortable one. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, with ten years of experience making AI useful. I'd probably be running something by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my job for a few years and get promoted, maybe to head of marketing operations, by being the person who automates everything. I'd invest steadily every month. Around year five I'd start my own business, depending on what looks good then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Genuinely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Getting promoted by automating everything could mean cutting colleagues. How does that sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair point. But I'd rather be the one making the call than the one it's made about. Getting promoted by automating my own team is not something I'm proud of, but in ten years nobody will be paid for the work my team does now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the calm turn into worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people side, still. Managing people through change is what I'm worst at, and that's the part that matters most in this one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, but not for me so much as for my team and my parents' friends. I'd land somewhere, but a lot of people with mortgages wouldn't. What would help is the government paying people while they retrain, and honest timelines from companies. I'm the person who'll be fine, and that makes me worry more about the people who won't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I want to manage people at all. These scenarios made me think my real skill is building things with the tools, not running a team. Maybe I'm in the wrong job already.

headlineQuote: I'm the person who'll be fine, and that makes me worry more about the people who won't.
portrait: Tomas is **27** and manages four people in marketing operations at a headphone and speaker company.
He uses **AI all day** and got the job for his systems skills, not his people skills.
He lives alone, has strong **savings**, and is comfortable taking risks.
As AGI nears he'd move from wages to **owning a business**, starting with refurbishing audio gear.
He expects to be fine and worries most about **colleagues with mortgages**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for his **team** and older people with mortgages.
